# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Review of "Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations"

**Bottom line:** This is the most useful document in the series. It tests durability within the same offices over time, which is what all four previous papers lacked. It registers the meetings test in advance and answers both the re-analysis and the meta-analysis directly. Its two main rebuttals hold: the gain is not entirely an artifact, and it does decay somewhat.

There are four main problems:
- The headline mediation shares do not match a simple time-accounting check on the paper's own figures.
- Control offices that cut their own meetings bias the decay estimate.
- The log-hours measure is ambiguously defined.
- One Halden reversion is labelled as a coverage case when it was not.

## Arithmetic

| Figure | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Per hour, logs, 24 months | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Decline in per-hour gain, like-for-like | 12.5 → 9.8 | −22%, described as "about a quarter" (acceptable) |
| Halden continuers, hours | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 | −13.4% ✓ |
| Halden continuers, per hour | 96.8 / 86.6 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Counter cost per contact | see §5 | stated 9%; first-pass check gives about 12% |

## 1. The mediation shares conflict with simple time accounting

Recurring meetings close no cases. So one direct check is to remove meeting time from the hours denominator and see how much per-hour gain is left. This uses the paper's own figures, and assumes control offices' hours stayed near 37.9 and that meetings fall within recorded working hours.

**Time outside recurring meetings, baseline to 24 months:**
- Treated: from 37.9 − 7.4 = 30.5 hours to 33.4 − 3.9 = 29.5 hours, a ratio of 0.966.
- Control: from 37.9 − 7.2 = 30.7 hours to 37.9 − 7.0 = 30.9 hours, a ratio of 1.007.
- Difference-in-differences: about −4.1%.

**Output per non-meeting hour:** output per FTE fell 3.4%, so output per non-meeting hour changed by 0.966 / 0.959 ≈ **+0.7%**.

On this accounting, the cut in recurring meetings accounts for roughly 90% or more of the 9.8% timesheet gain. Repeating the calculation with log hours gives about 100%. That leaves almost nothing for fatigue (18%) or the unexplained share (35%).

The registered model's 47% likely comes from regression across offices and months, which estimates association, not an accounting identity. Measurement error in the calendar data would also pull the meetings estimate down. Whatever the reason, the authors should:
- report the time-accounting decomposition alongside the model;
- explain why the two disagree; and
- note that the true meetings share may be well above 47%.

This matters for interpretation. The more the gain comes from reallocating time, the less of it reflects higher intensity of work or rest.

## 2. "Confirms" is too strong for the mediation test

Pre-registering the test was the right step. Three caveats remain:

- **The test is only partly confirmatory.** It was registered at month 11, after the month-6 exploratory finding and after 11 months of outcome data had been seen. If the model uses office-months from the whole 24 months, almost half the data overlap with the period that generated the hypothesis. Re-estimate it using months 12–24 only.
- **The effective sample is 14 offices, not the number of office-months.** Office-months within an office are not independent. The interval of 28% to 66% should come from inference that accounts for the small number of clusters, such as a wild cluster bootstrap.
- **The mediators were not randomised.** The limitations acknowledge this. Managers who cut meetings may also differ in other ways that affect output.

"Supports" would be accurate. "Confirms" is not.

## 3. Control-office contamination biases the decay estimate

In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their own meetings. Their output per hour then rose 4.1%. From that point on, the control group improves, so the difference-in-differences estimate is pushed down. Some of the apparent fall from 12.5% to 9.8% may therefore be the control group catching up, not the treatment effect fading.

The control offices' audit was plausibly prompted by the trial's own published meetings finding. The authors should report:
- the 24-month estimates excluding these two offices; and
- the treated offices' own trend from month 9 to month 24.

The contamination also complicates the claim that the gain persists. The fair comparison for policy is hours reduction plus reorganisation against reorganisation alone. That observation, which is suggestive and based on only two offices, may matter more than the decay estimate.

## 4. What do the system logs measure?

The paper describes the logs as recording "time staff are working on cases." If that is literal, log hours exclude meetings, and two problems follow.

- **The expected fall would be much smaller.** By the accounting in §1, case-work time fell only about 4–5% relative to control, not the reported 11%.
- **The mediation outcome means something different.** If meetings are not in the denominator of output per log-hour, the meetings pathway cannot work by reallocating time. It would have to work through something like fewer interruptions while doing case work.

The reported −11% suggests the logs actually measure something close to total logged-in time, including time during meetings. Please define the measure precisely. The interpretation that logs show "slightly more work than timesheets" depends on it.

## 5. The counter staffing and cost estimate needs its derivation

The county says restoring service would require 12% more staff and raise cost per contact by 9%. Neither figure is straightforward to reproduce.

- **Cost.** Twelve per cent more staff on unchanged pay raises the wage bill by 12%. Unless contacts handled rise above the pre-trial level, cost per contact rises by about 12%. Recovering abandoned calls might add around 4% to contacts handled, which could bring the figure to about 8%. The paper should show how 9% was reached.
- **Staffing.** With 12% more staff, staffed hours would be 1.12 × 0.83 ≈ 0.93 of the original. The estimate implicitly assumes the 6.7% per-hour gain persists once queues shorten. As noted in my review of the nine-month report, that gain was probably higher utilisation caused by longer queues, and it would shrink as queues fall. Fully restoring staffed hours requires about 20% more staff (1 / 0.83), so the county's estimate may be too low.

## 6. The Halden subset

- **Non-response.** Of 23 organisations contacted, 14 responded. The 9 that did not respond are not described, and they may include more reverters.
- **The baseline hours figure.** The 40.3-hour baseline is identical to the figure for the 27 organisations with time tracking in the Varga & Holm re-analysis. Is it this subset's own baseline? Also, do all 11 continuing organisations have time-tracking data?
- **The marketing agency is not a coverage case.** The Summary says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations." Marketing agencies were coded *discretionary* in the meta-analysis, and this one cited client deadlines. Two of the three reversions fit the coverage story; this one does not. The Summary should say so plainly.
- **"Upper bound" is worded inconsistently.** The text calls the figures an upper bound "for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them." That group is exactly what the figures describe, so they are not a bound for it. The intended meaning is presumably an upper bound for organisations generally. Also, with no comparison group, the bias could go in either direction.
- **The attrition question goes unanswered.** R. Okafor is a co-author of both this report and the original Halden paper. The re-analysis documented that seven of the nine withdrawals happened after the schedule began, contrary to the original paper. This report answers the re-analysis's other two claims but is silent on this one. It should address it.

## 7. Requests from earlier reviews still outstanding

- **Unit cost in case-processing.** Timesheet hours imply about 3.4 hours a week above schedule. If that is paid overtime, cost per case closed has risen, as discussed for the nine-month report. The county did this calculation for counters but not for case-processing.
- **Backlog and time to decision.** These are still not reported. At 24 months, compliance with statutory deadlines is the obvious measure of quality alongside appeal overturns.
- **Confidence intervals for secondary outcomes.** Sick days, resignations and overturn rates still lack them.

## 8. What the series now supports

| Question | Current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work | Real but modest: about 8.5–10% on randomised, record-based, actual-hours evidence at 24 months; about 12% in self-selected Halden survivors |
| Durable? | Mostly: it declined by roughly a quarter over 15 months, partly confounded by control offices cutting their own meetings |
| Output per worker | Slightly below control in discretionary work (−3.4%, confidence interval includes zero); hours cut mostly but not fully offset |
| Coverage-bound work | Does not pay: the counter arm was ended, and two of the three Halden reverters cited coverage |
| Mechanism | Mostly reallocation of time away from meetings, possibly more than the model's 47%; fatigue plays a minor role |
| Open question | Whether reorganising without cutting hours captures most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes the reorganisation happen and last |

The report's own unplanned observation identifies the next experiment: randomise offices to reduced hours, to a meeting audit at full hours, or to both.
